text: Classification is a label that tells people and systems how to handle data, without re-deciding the rules every single time. This lesson explains why that label has to exist at all, and sets up the rest of this chapter.

Without classification, an organization is stuck between two bad extremes. Protect everything at the highest level: encrypt every column, lock every table behind the strictest controls. It's safe, but enormously expensive, and most data was never that risky to begin with. Or protect everything at a light, average level: fast and cheap, but now customer Social Security numbers get the same casual handling as the cafeteria menu. Classification avoids both failure modes, applying strict, expensive controls only where sensitivity justifies the cost, and light controls everywhere else.

Classification is where Chapter 1's concepts stop being abstract. 'This column is sensitive' becomes 'this column is labeled Confidential.' 'This table contains PII subject to GDPR' becomes 'this table is labeled Restricted, access logged, encryption required.' The label is the bridge between a policy that says sensitive data must be protected, and a system that actually knows which rules apply to the dataset in front of it.

The rest of this chapter builds that bridge. Lesson 8 covers the actual schemes and labels, tiers like Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted. Lesson 9 covers discovering sensitive data in the first place. Lesson 10 covers applying classifications to real systems. Lesson 11 closes with classification governance, who decides the labels and keeps them current.
Without a label, every one of Chapter 1's concepts stays theoretical, true, but unenforceable. Next up: the actual schemes and labels organizations use.
